overall_feedback: The paper sets out a sensible symmetry-based experimental logic: a pristine centrosymmetric baseline, extrinsic inversion breaking by oxidation or etching, repeated sweeps that reveal a stochastic zero-field diode, field training, and a CDW-suppressed Ti-doped control. The pristine-device statistics (ten hBN-encapsulated devices with sub-0.5% upper bounds on eta) and the attention to sweep-to-sweep variability are real strengths, and the eta values quoted in Fig. S4 are arithmetically consistent with the listed Ic+ and Ic-. However, the central interpretation (metastable, CDW-inherited TRS-breaking domains) rests on inferences that the data do not yet isolate. (i) Ic+ and Ic- come from separate single-shot switching events whose own spread is comparable to the claimed diode asymmetry, so a random-sign eta with near-zero mean is also what one expects from ordinary switching-current statistics in an inhomogeneous, oxidized film; no switching histograms or signed-mean statistics are shown. (ii) Remanent magnet field and flux trapped during each resistive excursion are not excluded, and the out-of-plane training fields (0.1 to 0.2 T) are far above the thin-film vortex-entry scale, so the 'field selection' result is equally consistent with the conventional field-induced, vortex/edge-barrier diode effect; the Hc1 argument in Fig. S10 addresses only in-plane fields and uses a formula outside its validity range. (iii) The 1 T field-cooling result (stochasticity persists after field removal) sits uneasily with the claim that the domains are CDW-derived and field-selectable, and is not discussed. (iv) The Ti-doped null result lacks a positive control showing that inversion was actually broken in those devices (for example, a finite field-induced SDE), and Ti doping changes the superconducting state, disorder and critical currents, not only long-range CDW order. (v) With P along c from top-surface oxidation and an out-of-plane B_eff, the authors' own (P x B_eff) . I_c form vanishes, which needs to be addressed. There are also device-labeling inconsistencies between the main text and the Supplement that make it unclear which data come from oxidized versus etched samples, a large AC excitation relative to the reduced Ic, and a headline 83.61% value that comes from one of three sweeps. The conclusions in the abstract and Discussion ('reveal its time-reversal symmetry breaking origin', 'rooted in the CDW-related normal-state order') are stated more strongly than these controls support.

comments.title: Single-shot switching currents cannot separate a stochastic diode from ordinary switching-current scatter
comments.quote: where |𝐼𝑐+ | and |𝐼𝑐− | are defined as the onset currents of the superconducting-to-resistive
comments.explanation: Eq. (1) is the standard definition, and defining both Ic+ and Ic- as switching onsets from sweeps starting at zero bias is the right choice. My concern is statistical. In Fig. S4 the critical current itself moves a lot between consecutive sweeps: Ic+ is 36 uA in sweep #1 but 16.8 and 17.4 uA in sweeps #5 and #6, a factor of two change, while Ic- moves between 25.5 and 31.8 uA. Ic+ and Ic- are measured in separate half-sweeps at different times. If each branch's switching current has a spread of this size (as expected for phase-slip or hot-spot switching in an oxidized, multi-peak, inhomogeneous film), then any single (Ic+, Ic-) pair gives a nonzero eta of random sign even when the underlying distributions for the two polarities are identical. Random polarity with roughly zero mean, which is what Figs. 3d,e and S4 show, is exactly the signature of zero diode effect plus switching noise. I checked whether Fig. S12 resolves this: it shows the state is stable at fixed bias over 20 minutes, which rules out telegraph switching at fixed current, but it does not measure the distribution of switching currents over many sweeps of each polarity. Six sweeps per temperature (Fig. 3) and nine per field (Fig. 4) are too few to establish a distribution, and the signed mean of eta with its standard error is never reported. Without this, the claim that the device hosts a 'stochastic diode' rather than symmetric but noisy switching is not established.
comments.suggested_fix: For each device and condition, acquire N of at least 100 switching events for each polarity (alternating +/- sweeps), plot the Ic+ and Ic- histograms, and report the signed mean eta with its standard error together with a two-sample test (for example Kolmogorov-Smirnov) of whether the Ic+ and |Ic-| distributions differ; compare the sweep-to-sweep eta spread to the spread expected from the single-polarity Ic distributions alone.

comments.title: Remanent field and flux trapped during resistive excursions are not excluded as the source of stochastic polarity
comments.quote: Control measurements presented in Fig. S12 further rule out ordinary time-dependent
comments.explanation: The Fig. S12 control is useful for excluding telegraph noise at fixed bias. But the leading mundane explanation for a random-sign, field-trainable diode in a polar thin film is different: a small remanent field from the superconducting magnet (typically several mT to tens of mT after excursions to 1 T, which Figs. S8 and S9 involve) combined with vortices or flux that are trapped in new configurations every time the device is driven fully normal. Each sweep here runs to 300 uA, roughly ten times Ic of the oxidized devices, and the Fig. S12 normal-state voltage near 46 mV at 72 uA implies several microwatts of dissipation at dilution-refrigerator temperatures, so each sweep heats the film and re-cools it through Tc in whatever residual field is present. That reset mechanism gives a new pinned-flux landscape per sweep and naturally yields sweep-dependent eta of either sign, and an applied field of 0.1 to 0.2 T would then dominate and fix the sign. The manuscript does not state how true zero field was established, whether the magnet was degaussed, or how long the sample rested between half-sweeps. The Ti-doped null result partly argues against this, but those devices differ in pinning and Ic, so it is not decisive.
comments.suggested_fix: State the remanent field and how it was nulled (for example, by locating the field of maximum Ic or minimum |eta| in a fine Ic(B) scan near zero, or by quenching/degaussing the magnet), and repeat the zero-field stochastic measurement with the sweep amplitude limited to just above Ic and a fixed waiting time, reporting whether the polarity randomness persists when the device is never driven far into the normal state.

comments.title: Out-of-plane field 'stabilization' is also the conventional vortex/edge-barrier diode effect
comments.quote: external magnetic field selects and stabilizes the preexisting, metastable nonreciprocal state.
comments.explanation: I first read the Fig. S10 caption as the authors' answer to the vortex concern, since it concludes that 'field stabilization is not related to the vortex physics'. But that estimate concerns an in-plane field and the parallel lower critical field. The main-text training (Fig. 4, Device 13, and Fig. S11) uses out-of-plane fields of 0.1 to 0.2 T. For a thin film in perpendicular field the effective entry field is strongly reduced by demagnetization, and 0.1 to 0.2 T is a sizable fraction of the quoted perpendicular Hc2 of about 0.85 T, so vortices are certainly present. In a film with asymmetric edges (the zig-zag Device 13 is designed to have them), a perpendicular field produces a field-odd diode effect through asymmetric edge barriers or vortex pinning; this is the 'ubiquitous' thin-film SDE of Ref. 8. Such a field-induced contribution grows with |B| and would progressively fix first the sign and then the magnitude of eta, which is exactly the observed sequence at 0.1 T and 0.2 T. The data in Fig. 4 therefore do not distinguish 'selection of a preexisting TRS-broken domain state' from 'a conventional field-induced diode that overwhelms zero-field switching noise'.
comments.suggested_fix: Show eta(B) on a fine grid through zero (for example, steps of 5 mT from -50 to +50 mT) with many sweeps per point; a domain-selection picture predicts a finite, sign-locked |eta| that saturates at a small selection field and shows hysteresis on field reversal, whereas a conventional field-induced SDE predicts eta passing smoothly and linearly through zero without hysteresis. Also apply the same out-of-plane fields to the Ti-doped devices and report eta there.

comments.title: 1 T field cooling does not fix the polarity, which conflicts with CDW-derived trainable domains
comments.quote: and it is not eliminated by field-cooling followed by removal of the external field (Figs. S8 and
comments.explanation: The authors present this as further evidence that the diode is not a static artifact. However, it bears directly on their own interpretation. The CDW-related TRS-breaking order in CsV3Sb5 is reported to be trainable by field cooling through T_CDW (the Kerr work of Ref. 31, and Ref. 39 explicitly reports nonreciprocal critical currents with normal-state field trainability in this material). If the zero-field diode is governed by CDW-derived domains that a field can select, cooling in 1 T, much larger than the 0.1 to 0.2 T that fixes the polarity at base temperature, should leave a single-domain state and a reproducible zero-field polarity after the field is removed. Figs. S8 and S9 show that stochasticity persists. That points toward stabilization being a field-on effect (see the previous comment), or toward domains that are reset by each sweep and unrelated to the CDW chirality. The starting temperature of the field-cooling protocol is also not stated; cooling only from above Tc but below T_CDW (about 94 K) would not test CDW training.
comments.suggested_fix: State the temperature from which field cooling started, perform field cooling from above T_CDW (for example 120 K) in both +B and -B, and report whether the signed mean zero-field eta changes sign with the cooling-field sign; discuss explicitly how persistence of stochasticity after 1 T field cooling is reconciled with field-selectable CDW-derived domains and with Ref. 39.

comments.title: Ti-doped null result lacks a positive control that inversion was actually broken
comments.quote: After deliberately introducing inversion-symmetry breaking with the same
comments.explanation: The logic of the control is: same inversion-breaking protocol, no CDW, no diode, therefore the TRS-breaking ingredient is CDW-linked. For a null result to carry this weight, one must show that the protocol actually produced an effective polar axis in the Ti-doped devices. Oxidation kinetics and etch profiles may differ for a different composition, and the manuscript gives no Tc, Ic, thickness or normal-state resistance for Devices 15 and 16 to compare with Devices 11 to 14. The simplest positive control is available: a device with a polar axis should show a conventional field-induced SDE under an in-plane or out-of-plane field. If the Ti-doped devices show a finite eta(B) comparable to that of the undoped devices at 0.1 to 0.3 T but zero eta at B = 0, the control becomes strong; if they show no field-induced SDE either, the null result only shows that inversion breaking was ineffective. In addition, because the undoped stochastic SDE appears in only one of three sweeps at some oxidation stages, the number of sweeps taken on the Ti-doped devices matters and is not stated.
comments.suggested_fix: Report eta versus applied in-plane and out-of-plane field for Devices 15 and 16 (same fields as Figs. 4, S10 and S11), state the number of zero-field sweeps per oxidation or etch stage, and tabulate thickness, Tc, Ic and normal-state resistance for the Ti-doped devices next to Devices 11 to 14.

comments.title: Overclaim that the TRS breaking is CDW-derived 'rather than' superconducting
comments.quote: diode effect as related to the CDW-related electronic orders of the normal states, rather than the
comments.explanation: I agree the Ti-doped control is suggestive. But Ti substitution at x = 0.24 does not remove only long-range CDW order; it also changes the band filling, disorder, the superconducting dome and likely the pairing state. A TRS-breaking superconducting order parameter that exists only in the presence of CDW (or that is destroyed by the disorder and filling change of Ti doping) would give the same null result. So the control cannot discriminate 'inherited from the CDW' from 'a TRS-breaking condensate that requires the CDW-reconstructed Fermi surface'. Furthermore, Ref. 55 is titled 'Competitive charge density waves' in the doped compound, which suggests that short-range or competing CDW correlations may survive; the absence of a resistive kink only excludes a long-range transition. The abstract phrasing ('link superconducting-state TRS breaking to CDW-related order') is reasonable, but the Results and Discussion ('rather than the standalone superconducting condensate', 'rooted in the CDW-related normal-state order', 'reveal its time-reversal symmetry breaking origin') go further than a single-doping-level, two-device null result supports.
comments.suggested_fix: Replace 'rather than the standalone superconducting condensate' with a statement that the zero-field diode requires the presence of long-range CDW order at the doping levels studied, and note that a CDW-dependent TRS-breaking superconducting state is not excluded; ideally add an intermediate doping (for example x of about 0.05 to 0.1, where CDW survives with reduced T_CDW) to test whether the diode tracks T_CDW.

comments.title: Oxidation-induced polar axis along c gives zero in the authors' own (P x B_eff) . I_c form
comments.quote: thin flake, surface degradation, edges, and disorder naturally break inversion symmetry and
comments.explanation: The authors use (P x B_eff) . I_c (Ref. 3) to describe each local contribution. Top-surface oxidation of a flake mainly produces a polar axis P along the c axis. The CDW-related TRS-breaking signal invoked as the source of B_eff (polar Kerr, Refs. 31 and 34; muSR) is an out-of-plane (c-axis) orbital moment, and the domains are said to be trained by out-of-plane fields. With both P and B_eff along c, P x B_eff vanishes and the expression predicts no diode for in-plane current. A finite response then requires either an in-plane polar component (edges, lateral oxidation gradients, the zig-zag etch) or an in-plane component of B_eff. This matters because the paper presents oxidation and etching as two equivalent routes and uses Eq. (2) to interpret both; for the oxidized Devices 11 and 12 the relevant in-plane polar axis is never identified.
comments.suggested_fix: State explicitly that for in-plane current and c-axis B_eff the active polar component must lie in plane and perpendicular to I_c, identify its source in the oxidized devices (for example, lateral oxidation gradients from the flake edges, supported by the AFM maps of Fig. S5), and write Eq. (2) with the in-plane polar component P_j,parallel in place of P_j.

comments.title: AC excitation of 10 uA is comparable to the reduced critical currents
comments.quote: A DC bias current was supplied by a Yokogawa GS200 current source, while a small AC
comments.explanation: The Methods call the AC excitation 'small', but the Fig. S3 panels state Iac = 10 uA. After oxidation the critical currents fall to about 37 uA (Device 11) and to 17 to 36 uA (Fig. S4). An AC amplitude of 10 uA (peak about 14 uA if rms) is then 30 to 80% of Ic. The dV/dI onset then marks where I_dc plus the AC peak first reaches the switching current, so both onsets are shifted down by an amount of order the AC amplitude; this shrinks the denominator of Eq. (1) and inflates |eta|. The AC drive also repeatedly pushes weak links into the resistive state during the sweep, which is itself a source of sweep-to-sweep variability. For the 83.61% value, if |Ic+| is of order 37 uA then |Ic-| is of order 3 uA, smaller than the AC excitation, so the backward onset would be poorly defined; the Ic values behind Fig. 2c are not given. The excitation amplitude used for Devices 13 and 14 and for the dilution-refrigerator data is not stated.
comments.suggested_fix: Report Iac (rms or peak) and frequency for every data set, list |Ic+| and |Ic-| for Fig. 2c, and repeat the key eta measurements with Iac below 5% of Ic or with pure DC V-I sweeps using a voltage threshold criterion, showing that eta is unchanged.

comments.title: Headline 83.61% efficiency comes from one of three sweeps
comments.explanation: The main text presents 83.61% as the value Device 11 reaches at the second oxidation step, which a reader will take as a characteristic efficiency. The Supplementary Text says that at this stage three consecutive sweeps were taken and only the second showed an SDE, and that at the third stage none of three sweeps did. Given the paper's own emphasis on stochasticity, a single sweep out of three is the extreme of an unknown distribution rather than a property of the oxidized device. The same applies to Fig. 2d (one of three sweeps at the fourth stage). Reporting the selected sweep without the others in the main text gives an inflated picture of how large and how robust the oxidation-induced diode is.
comments.suggested_fix: State in the main text that 83.61% was obtained in one of three sweeps at that oxidation stage (the other two showing no detectable SDE), and report the eta values of all sweeps at each oxidation stage, for example as a table or by adding the non-SDE sweeps to Fig. 2.

comments.title: Device numbering differs between the main text and the Supplement
comments.quote: The same behavior appears in oxidized samples. Device 12, for example, shows sweep-to-
comments.explanation: The main text says Fig. 2 is oxidized Device 11, Device 12 is a second oxidized device with eta between -30.86% and 17.07% (Figs. S3 to S5), and Device 13 is the etched zig-zag device. In the Supplement, Fig. S3 is captioned 'Device 12 (Fig. 2 in the main text)' and the text around it describes the Fig. 2c,d oxidation stages, while Fig. S4, which contains exactly the 17.07%, -30.86% and -14.07% values, is captioned 'Device 13 after successive oxidation stages'. Fig. S6 is also labeled Device 13 but is cited for the etched device. A reader cannot tell whether the -30.86% to 17.07% data come from an oxidized or an etched device, and that matters because the claim that oxidation and etching independently produce the same stochastic behavior relies on it.
comments.suggested_fix: Use one device numbering across the main text and Supplement (for example, relabel Fig. S3 as Device 11 and Fig. S4 as Device 12 if the Supplement numbering is off by one), and add a table listing each device number, treatment (pristine, oxidized, etched, Ti-doped), thickness, Ic, and the figures in which it appears.

comments.title: Pristine baseline was not measured with the protocol that revealed the stochastic diode
comments.quote: Differential resistance measurements at 1.8 K show overlapping positive- and negative-bias
comments.explanation: The ten-device pristine baseline is a strength. But the activated devices show an SDE in only some sweeps (one of three, three of six), and much of the stochastic data are taken at 0.25 to 1.5 K in a dilution refrigerator. The pristine devices appear to be characterized at 1.8 K with what looks like a single forward and backward pair per device (Figs. 1e,f, S1, S2, Table S1). If the zero-field diode is intermittent, a single pair can miss it. Without a matched number of sweeps and temperature, the statement that pristine devices are diode-inactive and treated devices diode-active compares two protocols as well as two sample states. The pristine devices also have Ic of 81 to 496 uA, so the same absolute switching noise would give a much smaller eta there.
comments.suggested_fix: For at least two pristine encapsulated devices, report the distribution of eta over the same number of consecutive sweeps (at least the nine used in Fig. 4) at the same temperatures (0.25 to 1.5 K) and sweep rate (0.05 uA/s) as Device 13, and state how many sweeps underlie each Table S1 upper bound.

comments.title: Hc1 estimate in Fig. S10 is outside its validity range and the margin is not 'much larger'
comments.quote: estimated to be 0.59 T, according to the formula
comments.explanation: I checked the numbers: with mu0 Hc2,perp = 0.85 T, xi = sqrt(Phi0 / (2 pi mu0 Hc2)) gives 19.7 nm, and (2 Phi0 / (pi d^2)) ln(d/xi) with d = 40 nm gives about 0.59 T, so the arithmetic is right. But the thin-slab logarithmic formula assumes xi much smaller than d (and d much smaller than lambda); here d/xi is about 2, so ln(d/xi) is about 0.7 and the estimate is only good to order of magnitude. A factor of two between 0.59 T and the 0.3 T training field is then not 'much larger' and does not support the conclusion that field stabilization is 'not related to the vortex physics'. That conclusion also covers only the in-plane case; it says nothing about the out-of-plane training of Figs. 4 and S11. It is also unclear whether d = 40 nm and Hc2,perp = 0.85 T refer to Device 14 and at what temperature.
comments.suggested_fix: State that the parallel-field estimate is order-of-magnitude only because d/xi is about 2, specify the device and temperature for d and Hc2, restrict the conclusion to 'ordinary parallel vortex entry is not expected to dominate at 0.3 T in-plane', and remove the general statement that field stabilization is unrelated to vortex physics.

comments.title: Cited evidence for intact inversion includes a report of odd-parity order
comments.quote: global inversion symmetry is expected to remain intact in pristine AV3Sb5 at ambient
comments.explanation: The whole design depends on pristine CsV3Sb5 being centrosymmetric, and the null baseline supports it empirically. However, Ref. 35 (Asaba et al., 'Evidence for an odd-parity nematic phase above the charge-density-wave transition') reports an odd-parity, i.e. inversion-breaking, electronic phase, so it does not support the claim it is cited for. There are also proposals that some CDW stackings (for example, with a pi phase shift along c) can reduce the symmetry further. Citing this paper as support for intact inversion could mislead readers about the state of the literature, and the possibility of a weak intrinsic polar component that the oxidation merely domain-aligns is not discussed.
comments.suggested_fix: Remove Ref. 35 from the list supporting intact inversion, or cite it explicitly as a report of possible odd-parity order, and add a sentence noting that the pristine-device null result (Table S1, |eta| below 0.5%) bounds any intrinsic polar contribution at the resolution of these measurements.

comments.title: Earlier reports of field-free SDE and field trainability in CsV3Sb5 are not engaged
comments.quote: any claim of an intrinsic superconducting diode effect should be approached with caution.
comments.explanation: This sentence implicitly questions earlier work, notably Le et al. (Ref. 17), who reported a field-free SDE in CsV3Sb5 flakes, and Ge et al. (Ref. 39), who reported nonreciprocal critical currents with normal-state field trainability. Both are cited, but only in passing in the introduction. Readers need to know whether the present results contradict those works (for example, because those samples were not fully protected from oxidation, or had asymmetric geometries) or are consistent with them. Ref. 39 in particular reports trainability through the normal state, which appears to conflict with the persistence of stochastic polarity after 1 T field cooling reported here (Figs. S8 and S9).
comments.suggested_fix: Add a paragraph to the Discussion comparing device protection, geometry, sweep protocol and field-training procedure with Refs. 17 and 39, stating whether their zero-field signals could arise from extrinsic inversion breaking of the kind identified here, and how the field-cooling result of Figs. S8 and S9 relates to the normal-state trainability of Ref. 39.

comments.title: Eq. (2) assumes additive channel contributions, which does not match how a switching current is set
comments.quote: where 𝑗 labels superconducting paths or local domains and 𝑤𝑗 is the sweep-dependent weight
comments.explanation: Eq. (2) is presented as a heuristic, and I read it that way. Still, in an inhomogeneous network the onset of resistance is set by the first link or path that switches (a weakest-link or percolation process), not by a weighted sum of local diode efficiencies. In such a picture the measured eta is dominated by one or a few critical links, and a sign change between sweeps only requires a different link to be critical in the two polarities. That mechanism needs no TRS-broken domain reconfiguration, so the additive form makes the domain interpretation look more natural than the data require. Because the w_j are free and sweep-dependent, Eq. (2) can fit any observed eta and makes no testable prediction.
comments.suggested_fix: Label Eq. (2) explicitly as a qualitative model, and note that in a weakest-link picture eta is set by Ic+ = min_j Ic,j+ and Ic- = min_j Ic,j-, so that sign changes can arise from a change in which link is critical without any change in B_eff,j; state which observation (for example, field-odd hysteresis of the signed mean eta) would distinguish the two.

comments.title: Observing a field-free diode does not by itself show intrinsic TRS breaking
comments.quote: oxidation or asymmetric etching shows that the time-reversal symmetry is still broken.
comments.explanation: The symmetry statement is correct: a zero-field diode requires broken time-reversal symmetry somewhere. But the Discussion treats this as evidence for an internal electronic TRS-broken texture, with the only alternative considered being 'a permanent macroscopic magnetization'. Oxidation of a vanadium antimonide can create vanadium oxide surface layers or defects carrying local moments, and those need not be ferromagnetic or macroscopic to supply an effective exchange field near the surface. Trapped flux and remanent field (see the earlier comment) are other extrinsic TRS-breaking sources. The etched Device 13 shows the effect without heavy oxidation, which helps, but etched edges in air also oxidize. So 'TRS is broken' is established, while 'the TRS breaking is intrinsic to CsV3Sb5' is not established by this step alone.
comments.suggested_fix: Rephrase to 'shows that a time-reversal-breaking field is present in the measured state' and add a sentence acknowledging oxidation-generated local moments and trapped flux as extrinsic alternatives, citing the Ti-doped control (with the positive control requested above) as the evidence against them.
